purpose: Pamidronate is used to treat high calcium levels in the blood, which can happen with certain cancers. It is also used to strengthen bones that have been weakened by cancer that has spread to the bones, or by conditions like Paget's disease. It helps reduce bone pain and lowers the risk of bone fractures.
how_it_works: Your bones are constantly being broken down and rebuilt. In some conditions, the breakdown happens too fast, causing bones to weaken and calcium to leak into the blood. Pamidronate works by slowing down the cells that break bones apart, giving your bones a chance to stay stronger. This also helps keep calcium levels in your blood at a safer level.
common_side_effects: Fever, chills, or flu-like feelings within the first day or two after your infusion. You may also notice tiredness, nausea, bone or muscle aches, low calcium levels (causing tingling or muscle cramps), and redness or swelling at the injection site.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, as this medicine can affect your kidneys — your doctor will monitor your kidney function regularly. A rare but serious side effect called osteonecrosis of the jaw (jaw bone damage) has been reported, so keep up with dental care and tell your dentist you are on this medicine. Avoid dental procedures if possible during treatment. Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as this medicine is not recommended during pregnancy.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given by a slow intravenous (IV) infusion directly into a vein, usually in a clinic or hospital setting. The dose and how often you receive it depends on your condition — for example, for high calcium it may be given as a single infusion, while for bone disease related to cancer it may be given once a month. Each infusion typically takes 2 to 24 hours. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you.
